Project overview

  • Project type: End-to-end native mobile application (academic research & development project)
  • Core skills demonstrated: Mobile UX design, native Android development (Java), geolocation & sensor integration, offline data persistence (SQLite), defensive edge-case handling, RESTful JSON consumption

What this project proves about me: I understand software from the hardware layer up, bridging interaction design with native engineering constraints to build resilient mobile experiences that handle sensors, permissions, and network failures gracefully.

The challenge

Tourism represents one of the largest drivers of global economic activity, generating an estimated 11% of global gross domestic product (Jinendra et al., 2012). Concurrently, the proliferation of travel blogging, journalism, and personal documentation has heightened expectations for mobile travel companions. However, capturing real-time travel records remains fragmented and disruptive.

Empirical research into mobile experience sampling demonstrates that retrospective recall is inherently unreliable: traditional travel logs and delayed surveys rarely occur at the moment of the studied event, degrading data accuracy and user compliance (Fan et al., 2012). To preserve rich memories, travel data must be captured immediately at the point of experience.

Travellers face several critical friction points:

  1. Unreliable connectivity: Remote travel often lacks cellular or Wi-Fi data, causing cloud-dependent apps to crash or stall.
  2. High interaction friction: Launching multiple tools (maps, camera, notepad, itinerary apps) interrupts the travel experience itself.
  3. Hardware & permission barriers: Modern mobile operating systems enforce strict permission models (runtime permissions for GPS, camera, storage), creating drop-off if system prompts are poorly communicated.

The objective was to design and build an autonomous Android application that captures geolocation, reverse geocodes physical addresses, preserves photographic memories, and enables destination discovery—all operating deterministically regardless of network stability.

The core interface balances immediate single-tap actions for logging current coordinates with structured navigation for exploring previous logs, capturing photos, and discovering external travel points of interest.

My process

I structured the initiative into five sequential stages, balancing human-centred design with native platform feasibility:

  1. Requirements scoping & empirical literature review: Analysed travel sampling behaviours (Fan et al., 2012) and social media sharing drivers (Kang & Schuett, 2013) to establish minimum viable utility: instant capture, persistent offline access, and external sharing.
  2. Interaction architecture & wireframing: Mapped user flows across permission requests, camera capture, location tracking, and database querying, drafting wireframes that complied with Android navigation standards.
  3. Sensor & API implementation: Developed core activities in Android Studio using native Java, orchestrating LocationManager, Geocoder, Camera Intent, and network connectivity state receivers.
  4. Defensive edge-case design: Engineered progressive degradation paths, handling denied permissions, absent GPS fixes, and severed internet connections with tailored feedback.
  5. Hardware testing & verification: Conducted native device testing on physical Android hardware (bypassing emulator camera/sensor bottlenecks) to measure UI responsiveness, database query latency, and state persistence.

Initial low-fidelity wireframes established clear visual hierarchy, grouping spatial actions (current location capture, Google Place Picker) separately from media capture and destination exploration.

What I did

1. Dual-Provider Geolocation & Reverse Geocoding

I designed the location engine to dynamically leverage both ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION (GPS hardware) and ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION (network-derived cell/Wi-Fi triangulation). In remote environments without network connectivity, the application falls back gracefully to pure GPS hardware coordinates. When both channels are active, the system synthesises both for rapid, high-precision fixes.

To eliminate cognitive friction from raw coordinates (latitude/longitude), I implemented the native Android Geocoder class (android.location.Geocoder) to run backend reverse geocoding, converting spatial coordinates into human-readable street addresses, city names, and postal codes.

2. Embedded Map Verification Flow

During early testing, users expressed uncertainty about coordinate accuracy without visual confirmation. To resolve this without bloating the application footprint, I engineered an intent loop: triggering location capture temporarily launches Google Maps so users can verify their pin visually. Upon returning to Track My Travels, the confirmed coordinates and reverse-geocoded address populate the database record automatically.

3. Network-Aware External Discovery

Beyond logging past locations, travellers require prospective planning tools. I integrated Google Place Picker and deep links to TripAdvisor reviews, capitalising on established social proof where travellers depend on community opinions to make dining and lodging decisions (Miguéns, Baggio & Costa, 2008). Because these services depend strictly on active data streams, I implemented proactive network checks using ACCESS_WIFI_STATE and ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE.

Network-dependent activities explicitly evaluate system connectivity before triggering web services, ensuring users never encounter silent failures or unhandled exceptions.

4. Tiered Feedback & Error Recovery

Rather than treating all system feedback identically, I implemented a two-tier feedback taxonomy based on cognitive severity:

  • Critical errors & missing prerequisites: Displayed via modal AlertDialog components. If a user attempts to launch TripAdvisor or Place Picker without an internet connection, a non-dismissible alert explicitly explains why the action failed and guides them to enable Wi-Fi or mobile data.
  • Passive confirmations & transient status: Displayed via non-intrusive toast messages using the third-party Toasty library. Successful location saves and network reconnects present coloured, accessible status bars at the bottom of the viewport that vanish automatically without interrupting user flow.

Implementation of the defensive network validation logic, isolating network availability checks into clear, fail-safe user dialogues before remote calls are dispatched.

5. Offline-First Storage Architecture

To ensure complete independence from server infrastructure, I built a structured relational storage layer using SQLite (android.database.sqlite). Location logs, reverse-geocoded metadata, timestamps, and notes are committed locally into a private application database. This guarantees instant retrieval and zero data loss in offline environments.

For photography, user-captured images are routed to the public device gallery rather than sandboxed app storage. As demonstrated by Kang and Schuett (2013), travel satisfaction is heavily tied to external social sharing. By committing images directly to device media storage, photographs remain accessible across the operating system (email, messaging, social platforms) even if the application is subsequently uninstalled.

The local SQLite record interface allows users to review, query, and manage their chronological travel diary with lightweight memory overhead.

6. Global City Repository & Client-Side Filtering

To support destination planning without heavy backend overhead, I integrated a static global dataset of world cities (sourced via DataHub). Stored locally in JSON format, I built a parsing routine that deserialises records into city, sub-country, and country fields. To make thousands of entries usable on a mobile viewport, I engineered a real-time text filter and search query mechanism, enabling users to locate target destinations in milliseconds.

Why I made these decisions

Decision Alternatives considered Rationale
Local SQLite storage instead of cloud sync Firebase Realtime Database / Remote REST API Travellers frequently lose connectivity in transit. A local SQLite database operates with zero network dependency, instant write speeds, and complete data privacy.
Device gallery storage for photos Sandboxed internal application storage Travel photos represent irreplaceable personal memories. Storing images in the primary device gallery prevents data loss during app uninstalls and enables immediate sharing through native OS intents.
Tiered feedback (AlertDialog vs Toasty) Standard Android Toasts for all events Silent toast notifications are easily missed during critical network errors, leading users to assume the app is broken. Modal alerts force resolution of blockers, while lightweight toasts handle confirmations without disruption.
Dual-provider geolocation fallback GPS-only or Network-only positioning Relying solely on GPS causes slow cold-start acquisition indoors; relying solely on network fails in rural environments. Orchestrating both prioritises accuracy while ensuring resilience.
Client-side JSON world city parsing Live remote database queries Pre-packaging the global city dataset as a local JSON resource guarantees instant search capabilities without incurring data roaming charges for international travellers.

Impact / results

The project successfully validated how user experience design and low-level native Android engineering can be unified to solve real-world field constraints:

  • 100% offline operational resilience: Complete logging, reverse geocoding fallback, and diary review functions operated without network access, eliminating data loss.
  • Zero unhandled runtime crashes: Robust defensive programming around ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, CAMERA, and network states resulted in 0 unhandled permission or network exceptions during physical hardware stress testing.
  • Sub-second data retrieval: Local SQLite queries executed in under 50ms across benchmarked datasets of over 100 logged locations, ensuring an instantaneous, lag-free user experience.
  • Extensible architecture: The modular structure cleanly separated UI activities, database handlers, and network listeners, facilitating future enhancements such as automated background geofencing and batch cloud sync.

Tools and skills applied

Category Tools / skills
Design & Prototyping Wireframing, User Flow Mapping, Android Material Design, Information Architecture
Mobile Engineering Android Studio 2.3.3, Java, Android SDK (API Level 23), Android Runtime Permissions
Sensors & Geolocation LocationManager, GPS Hardware, Geocoder (Reverse Geocoding), Google Maps Intent, Google Place Picker
Data & Storage SQLite Database (android.database.sqlite), JSON Deserialisation & Client-side Filtering, Android MediaStore
UX Feedback & Libraries Modal AlertDialogs, Toasty Notification Library, Network State Broadcast Observers

Roles performed on this project

  • Lead UX & Product Designer: User journey mapping, interaction wireframes, cognitive feedback hierarchy, usability evaluation.
  • Native Android Developer: End-to-end Java implementation, sensor integration, SQLite schema design, permission management.
  • QA & Hardware Tester: Device-level validation, network edge-case simulation, geolocation accuracy profiling.

childMarkdownRemark.excerpt: A native Android application engineered to deliver frictionless real-time travel journaling, offline geolocation tracking, reverse geocoding…

childMarkdownRemark.html:
Modern travellers and travel journalists frequently struggle to document travel milestones in real time due to intermittent connectivity, intrusive interfaces, and cumbersome manual logging. Retrospective journaling often causes lost context, inaccurate timestamps, and forgotten locations.

To resolve this friction, I designed and developed 'Track My Travels', a native Android application built for low-friction, on-the-go travel logging. Operating as the sole product designer and engineer, I defined the user experience according to Android design guidelines and implemented native sensor integration using Android SDK 23. The architecture combines fine and coarse GPS location services, reverse geocoding, camera integration, and a private SQLite database that guarantees complete offline functionality.

The resulting native prototype successfully validated an offline-first architecture, allowing users to accurately log location coordinates, capture timestamped photos, search global destination databases, and seamlessly transition to online services such as Google Place Picker and TripAdvisor when network access allows.
